analysis.one_liner: Blocks federal credit card consumer-protection rules and replaces them with disclosure-only requirements.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have stopped new Federal Reserve credit card rules from taking effect, was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In January 2009, federal banking regulators issued rules restricting credit card practices considered unfair to cardholders, such as certain rate increases and fee arrangements. This bill would have barred the Federal Reserve, the Office of Thrift Supervision, and the National Credit Union Administration from putting those rules into effect, and in their place required only clearer disclosures and 75 days' advance written notice before most changes to card terms. It was introduced by Representative Jeb Hensarling with 19 Republican cosponsors in May 2009 and died in committee without any committee vote or House floor action.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, credit card issuers would have benefited most: they could have continued raising interest rates on existing balances, applying payments to benefit the issuer, and charging fees the new rules restricted, while facing only lighter disclosure duties. Issuers argued the rules would limit access to credit and raise prices for responsible borrowers.

how_it_helps.text: Bars the Federal Reserve, the Office of Thrift Supervision, and the National Credit Union Administration from implementing the credit card rule published in the Federal Register on January 29, 2009, or any substantially similar rule based on an unfairness determination.

Requires card issuers to give clear disclosures about payment timing, how payments are applied across balances with different rates, rate increases, the two-cycle average daily balance method, and account-opening fees.

Requires 75 days' advance written notice before changes to those terms take effect, with exceptions for rate increases driven by an outside index or the expiration of a previously disclosed promotional rate.

analysis.who_pays: Cardholders would have borne the cost if the bill passed: the practices the regulators' rule restricted — including certain rate increases on existing balances and fee structures — would have remained legal with only a notice requirement, so households carrying credit card debt would have kept paying for them.

drawbacks.text: The bill's centerpiece is purely negative: it prohibits agencies from acting, rather than setting new substantive protections, so cardholders would be left to protect themselves by reading disclosures rather than by enforceable limits on practices.

Supporters' good-faith argument was that the January 2009 rules restricted pricing and risk management in ways that could raise rates or reduce credit availability for everyone, including borrowers who pay on time; replacing restrictions with disclosures preserves issuer flexibility. The bill acknowledges this trade-off by keeping rate-setting with issuers.

Even the disclosure provisions leave exceptions: no advance notice is required when a rate rises because of an outside index or a promotional rate expiring, exactly the situations where cardholders most often see surprise increases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades enforceable restrictions on credit card practices for paperwork. Clearer disclosures and 75 days' notice are real, modest benefits, but the core provision would have undone regulatory rules limiting practices the agencies had determined were unfair, leaving cardholders with information but no protection. The disclosure provisions are also narrower than the rules they would displace.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died at the end of the Congress without a hearing, a vote, or floor action.

narrative.text: Representative Jeb Hensarling introduced the bill on May 7, 2009, with 19 Republican cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The action history shows no further steps: no committee markup, no report, and no floor vote in the House or Senate before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

The rules the bill targeted — the credit card rule published in the Federal Register on January 29, 2009 — restricted practices the regulators had determined were unfair, such as certain rate increases and payment-allocation methods.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card holders came out ahead, because the effort to block the regulators' credit card rules never advanced, leaving the consumer protections free to take effect. Card issuers, who would have kept more freedom to raise rates and charge fees had the bill passed, lost the chance instead.

for.name: Rep. Jeb Hensarling
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to block the January 2009 credit card rules and replace them with disclosure requirements.

for.name: 19 of 178 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat cosponsored it.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup or reported it out, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never advanced in the Democratic-controlled House.

industries.note: The bill would have voided regulators' restrictions on practices found unfair — including certain rate increases on existing balances and payment-application methods — leaving issuers free to use them with only disclosure and notice duties. Their gain would have come directly from cardholders' continued costs, but the bill died before any of this took effect.

The bill would have barred the National Credit Union Administration from implementing the same January 2009 rule, freeing credit union card programs from its restrictions; cardholders at credit unions would have faced the same practices as other cardholders.
